sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- web_search: Web research. Prefer {queries:[...]} with 2-4 varied angles; omit provider unless overriding the default.
- source_check: Gather source evidence with passage citations for a claim.
- fetch_content: Use to fetch URL content, direct images, GitHub repos, and videos.
- get_search_content: Use after web_search, source_check, or fetch_content to read stored content; findText finds passages without paging.
- permissions: Read or change toolsets, path scope, and sandboxes (asks the user to confirm)

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Before each ask tool call, state the action and its specific purpose, including in subagents. Call the tool directly. Approval resumes that same call.
- For off tools, request set_toolset only if the permissions toolset is on. Never bypass a refusal.
- If a subagent uses ask_parent for a permission change, call permissions with the requested action and wait for user consent. Resume the child with the result. A child request is not user consent.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

sections.project_context:
<project_context>
Project-specific instructions and guidelines:

<project_instructions path="/home/fira/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md">
use typescript, bun, vite.

on naming, use snake case, verb noun for actions, predicate for bools, plural for iterables and records

for coding style, prefer functional programming, be modular and cohesive

prefer self explanatory code over commenting

use function statement for named functions

use type, no interface

use modern tech such as es module

do not build or test

## Web app libraries

- Render components with `h(component, props, ...children)`. Do not call component functions directly (e.g. `h(button, { label })`, not `button({ label })`). This lets React invoke components and preserves hook behavior. `h` is from `lib/web/hyperscript.ts` and is installed globally by the web prelude.
- `h(tag, props?, ...children)` also accepts DOM tags. String tags can include classes, e.g. `h('div.panel', props, child)`.
- `use_state`, `use_ref`, `use_effect`, and `use_mount` from `lib/web/react.ts` are project hook wrappers. `use_state` returns `[value, set_value]`; calling the setter with no argument toggles a boolean. Effects can return cleanup functions.
- `s(initial_value, options)` from `lib/web/state.ts` declares shared state and returns a hook. Options used in this app include `localstorage` and `url_param`; `init_localstorage_prefix(name)` scopes persisted keys.
- `use_keyboard(key, handler, options)` from `lib/web/use keyboard.ts` registers a shortcut; use `when` for conditional activation.
- `use_sync_theme` and `use_window_active` are hooks from `lib/web/use sync theme.ts` and `lib/web/use window active.ts`.
- The web prelude `lib/web/global.ts` installs React, web helpers, and shared utilities as globals. For an unfamiliar unimported name, check the prelude and its defining module; don't assume it is a React built-in.
- tsconfig path starts from source, not source/web

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: web_search
toolsAdded.description: Search the web for sources or answers. Full results are stored for retrieval with get_search_content by responseId. Prefer 2-4 varied queries.

queries.description: Run concurrently (up to three at a time); vary the angle

model.description: Model ID; needs provider openai, gemini, xai, mistral

provider.description: auto, all, a name, or comma-separated names; omit for the configured default.

workflow.description: Default none; summary-review opens the curator; auto-summary summarizes

proxy.description: Proxy URL; omit by default (env proxy vars ignored); "" forces direct

toolsAdded.name: source_check
toolsAdded.description: Gather cited web passages about a claim for manual review.

fetchContent.description: Fetch top 5 pages for exact passages

provider.description: auto, all, a name, or comma-separated names; omit for the configured default.

proxy.description: Proxy URL; omit by default; "" forces direct

toolsAdded.name: fetch_content
toolsAdded.description: Fetch web pages, PDFs, GitHub repos, images, YouTube and local video, as the mode allows. Full content is stored for retrieval with get_search_content.

forceClone.description: Clone GitHub repos over the size limit

prompt.description: Question for video analysis or answer mode

mode.description: readable (default): extract readable content as markdown; raw: return the exact textual body using direct HTTP only; answer: answer a prompt using only fetched content.

timestamp.description: Video frame time ('1:23:45') or range ('23:41-25:00'); needs ffmpeg

frames.description: Frames over a range, 5s apart from one time, or over the video

auth.description: authFetch profile name, or true for the only one

proxy.description: Proxy URL; omit by default; "" forces direct

toolsAdded.name: get_search_content
toolsAdded.description: Page through or search stored content from web_search, source_check, or fetch_content by responseId.

toolsAdded.name: permissions
toolsAdded.description: Read or change the toolsets, path scope, and bash sandboxes. Every change asks the user to confirm.

action.description: Action to run. Read status first when the reason for a block is unclear.

enabled.description: Legacy on/off value for set_toolset, or value for set_sandbox.

mode.description: set_toolset: off, on, ask. Filesystem: off, read, read+write. Use mode or enabled, not both.

reason.description: What the call does and why it is needed.

scope.description: project: project root only. custom: project root plus saved extra paths. everywhere: no path limit.

path.description: Directory for add_path, remove_path, add_mount, and remove_mount.

writable.description: add_mount: true mounts the directory read-write, so the sandboxed tools can change it.

name.description: Toolset name for add_toolset, remove_toolset, and set_toolset.

patterns.description: Regular expression sources for add_toolset, tested against tool names.

thread state machine

# intent

you may

- subscribe (read) a thread
- leave an opened thread
- new thread
- init thread
- send message on existing thread
- config tools
- call a pending tool
- generate

everything should be in sync by default as in data, wo relying on memory or specific control flows, via websocket.

# structure

thread structure

```yaml
tree: root | message -> children: message[], focus?: message
  0: # 0 is always 0, representing root
    children:
      - foo
    focus: foo
  foo:
    children: []
    focus:
  1: # title naming
    children:
      - bar
    focus: bar
  2: # web search
    children:
      - asdf
    focus: asdf
roots: root -> config
  0:
    model?: provider_model
    system_prompt?:
    tools?: tool name[]
    # you may shift starting position after compact
    start?: node
    pending_tools?: tool -> tool structure
messages: message -> message structure
```

thread state

```yaml
is_active?: # whether there is ongoing streaming msg/tool
```

thread index

```yaml
# id:
title:
folder:
is_hidden?:
creation_time: 
modification_time: 
```

thread history: jsonl of type, time, payload

message history: jsonl of type, time, payload

server history: plain text log

message structure

```yaml
# id:
role:
content:
reasoning?:
tools?: tool structure[]
start_time:
end_time:
usage?:
  prompt_tokens:
  completion_tokens:
  total_tokens:
perf?:
  tokens_per_second:
  time_to_first_token:
metadata?:
  has_failed?:
  model?:
  tags?:
```

tool structure

```yaml
tool:
args: # just nest a bit to be simple
  ...
```

# actions

you process actions on backend.

```
call tool {tool id}
  msg id

  append message

  broadcast set message, set tree

  broadcast append message
    content

  broadcast finish message
```

```
subscribe thread
  add client

  thread struture = read thread || empty thread

  broadcast set thread structure thread structure to client

unsubscribe thread
  rm client # ws is stable for the same client across events

init thread options
  thread structure = empty thread structure + scaffolding options

  commit to db (both thread and index)

  broadcast set thread structure

send prompt thread prompt # send
  message = random id

  message structure =
    role user
    content prompt
    ...

  append message

  broadcast set message, set tree

# thread status...
# in memory pending msgs content...

generate thread
  msg id

  append message

  broadcast set message, set tree

  build plain context

  generate_mock context, options, receive

  receive event
    if append
      # payload = delta

      # append to pending msgs...
      broadcast append message thread message delta
    if finish
      # payload = message structure

      commit to db

      broadcast finish message thread message message structure
```

# broadcasts

you sync w broadcasts on frontend.

```
set thread structure thread thread structure

# set thread config, metadata...

set tree thread tree

set message thread messge

append message thread message delta

finish message thread message message structure

# set thread status status: 'ready' | 'pending'
```

# abstractions

## naming

```
thread: thread id
thread_content: serialized thread text
thread_structure: in memory thread object, incl.
  tree: message ->
    children: []
    focus: message = first children
  # specifically,
  # for leaf,
  # children: []
  # focus: nil
  # for stem,
  # children: [foo, bar]
  # focus: foo
  message: message -> message structure
  metadata
    title
    folder
    time...
  config: # current config
    system prompt
    model
    provider
message: message id
message_content
message_structure:
  id?
  role
  content
  time...
  has_failed?
plain_message_structure:
  role
  content
context: message_structure[]
plain_context: plain_message_structure[] # payload to endpoint
delta:
  content
  reasoning?
```

<!-- it doesnt matter which one you make simpler. -->

## utils

```
append node tree message -> new tree

set focus tree message -> new tree

build context thread structure

build plain context thread structure

append message thread structure -> new structure
  append node
  set message
```

## web

```
# binds reconnect, setup heartbeat
connect

controls: control -> fn # behavior of each button/shortcut/command

# payload includes thread message if available. no default currying.
await perform(action, payload, timeout) -> response

# filter irrelevant broadcasts yourself
broadcasts: broadcast action -> fn # state transition for each broadcast
```

## backend

```
actions: action -> fn # response for each user action, e.g. build state from persistent storage and in memory cache (e.g. ongoing msg), mutate state if appliable

# seems broadcasts are always thread specific, only broadcast to subscribers in the first place
# thread is included in payload to be general, err when both client and thread in payload non existing
await? broadcast(broadcast, payload, client = all subs of this thread)

respond(request, payload, client)

send(client, payload)
  ws.send(stringify(payload))
```

## payload

request (i.e. user action)

```
type: request
request: request id
action
payload
```

response

```
type: response
request: request id
payload
```

broadcast

```
type: broadcast
event:
payload
```

# flow

## open the app

connect to ws

- auto reconnect
- heartbeat

list all threads

```
action: list
```

## open a thread

~~for empty thread, do nothing~~

subscribe (read) the read

```
action: subscribe thread

# for non existing thread, set an empty template
broadcast: set thread structure
```

you always subscribe a thread and decouple thread and displayed thread on url.

```
thread = nil
displayed thread = nil bind url

app(){
  thread = display thread ?? random id

  if displayed thread = nil
    displayed thread = thread if there are some messages

  thread will be always present. you ignore nil thread (init...).
}
```

## new thread

set thread random id

## send message

```
if no messages,
  # do it on frontend to make it easier to work w options
  action: init thread options

action: send thread prompt options

action: generate thread options
```

you will receive any change on the current thread

```
broadcast: set thread structure

# e.g. model, role, start time... you dont wanna include all these on any "append"
broadcast: set message

broadcast: append message...

# full message structure as if non streaming
broadcast: finish message
```

# controls

```
new thread
  set thread random id

send
  init if needed
  
  send prompt

  generate
```

# rationale

you always chat on root 0.

when you compact, you start a compact workflow on new root, inject the result to root 0, and shift starting point instead.

that's one of the main approaches.


--- tools ---
tools

# intent

given a set of tools, 

inject their instructions into system prompt when building context,

parse tool calls when finish, 

append to pending tool calls and sync w frontend.

when approved, call the fn of such tools,

(otherwise cancel or ignore)

stream their output into some message just like llms,

set and sync ready state when finish (or when they all finish if many).

when the last msg is tool (or user) and it's ready and there is no pending tool call (start if any),

start the next generation.

# spec

thread structure

see archi thread.

---

have tool calls in yaml.

---

on build context, combine consecutive messages of the same role and consider tool as user

# rationale

you can really have dynamic tools.

but let's make it fixed. generally you would have a set of "current enabled" tools on every thread, at least on ux. root 0 is the main user thread.

that's easier to implement, and beneficial on cost (input cache) out of box. and modern llms can really handle it anyway, generally speaking.

---

rather have no metadata when you do not define any, esp when you even have no way to define programmatically.

you can always add new fields and existing code will work (as long as they dont take as a whole and parse everything).

---

```tool
web_search:
  query: foo
```

## Current architecture

- **`source/web/component/app.ts`** owns thread/UI state and sends a `send` → `generate` action sequence over WebSocket. It handles thread/message broadcasts, but has no tool-call state or approval/call action.
- **`source/backend/serve.ts`** implements WebSocket actions and broadcasts. `generate` builds plain context, streams a response, and persists the finished assistant message.
- **`source/utility/generate.ts`** parses OpenAI-compatible SSE, but currently only reads text and reasoning deltas. Both `complete()` implementations have placeholder comments for parsing tools.
- **`source/utility/thread.ts`** builds the focused conversation path. `build_plain_context` currently sends only `{ role, content }`, so it would drop assistant tool calls and tool results.
- **`drafts/archi thread.md`** describes thread synchronization through persisted state and broadcasts, including actions for calling pending tools and a thread-ready status.
- **`drafts/archi tools.md`** proposes injecting enabled tool instructions into context, parsing tool calls, keeping them pending until approved, streaming tool output, and generating again when the thread is ready.

## Plan

1. **Define the tool contract and thread state**
   - Settle the persisted representation for tool calls, tool results, and pending/approved/cancelled status.
   - Add thread config for enabled tools, plus a clear ready/active indicator.
   - Decide whether tools are fixed server-side to start, as suggested in the tools draft, or configured per thread. Keep execution separate from model-supplied arguments.

2. **Preserve provider tool-call data**
   - Extend `generate` to send enabled tool definitions in the OpenAI-compatible request.
   - Parse streamed `tool_calls` deltas by call index, accumulating IDs, names, and argument JSON across chunks.
   - Return completed calls with the assistant message and persist/broadcast them through `finish_message`.
   - Handle malformed or incomplete arguments as generation errors rather than executing them.

3. **Make context tool-aware**
   - Update context construction so assistant tool-call messages and tool-result messages survive serialization to the provider.
   - Inject definitions/instructions only for tools enabled on the thread.
   - Follow the draft’s role/message normalization strategy, but confirm how it maps to the provider’s required tool-call and tool-result format before implementing.

4. **Add a safe tool execution lifecycle**
   - Introduce a backend action to approve/call a pending tool, and optionally a cancellation action.
   - Validate tool name and arguments against the server’s registry; never execute arbitrary names or code from model output.
   - Run the selected handler, persist its result as a tool message, and broadcast state changes.
   - Keep tools requiring approval pending until explicitly approved; define failure and timeout behavior.

5. **Resume generation after tool results**
   - Once all tool calls for the assistant turn have completed (and none remain pending), generate again with the updated context.
   - Prevent duplicate execution or overlapping generation if a request is retried or multiple clients act concurrently.
   - Expose active/ready state so reconnecting clients can recover the current lifecycle from thread state, not transient UI memory.

6. **Wire the UI to synchronized state**
   - Add broadcasts for tool-call updates and thread status, and handle them in `app.ts`.

Here are the main decisions to settle before implementation, roughly in dependency order:

1. **Tool protocol**
   - Which provider format to support first: OpenAI-compatible `tool_calls`, or a provider-neutral internal format with adapters?
   - Should streaming tool-call deltas be assembled in `generate`, or should generation return raw provider events for another layer to parse?

2. **Tool inventory**
   - Which tools ship first, and what exact handlers do they invoke?
   - Are tools registered in a fixed server-side registry, or can a thread configure its available tools?
   - Are tool definitions and instructions maintained in code, or loaded from configuration?

3. **Approval policy**
   - Which tools require user approval, and can any run automatically?
   - Does approval apply to each call, or can the user grant ongoing permission?
   - What does “cancel” mean: reject this call, or stop the whole assistant turn?

4. **Persisted call and result shape**
   - What fields must a call store? At minimum: provider call ID, tool name, arguments, and status.
   - How are results represented in the conversation: dedicated `role: 'tool'` messages, or nested on the call?
   - How are failures, malformed arguments, timeouts, and rejected calls represented?

5. **Conversation/context format**
   - Should tool calls/results follow the provider’s native message structure in persisted context, or be converted from a provider-neutral representation on each request?
   - How should consecutive tool results and multiple calls be grouped?
   - Confirm how the draft’s “tool as user” rule fits the provider’s expected format.

6. **Execution lifecycle**
   - When exactly should follow-up generation start: after each result, or after every call from the assistant message finishes?
   - Can independent calls in one response run concurrently?
   - How do we prevent duplicate execution and duplicate follow-up generation after retries or multiple connected clients?

7. **Thread status and recovery**
   - Which statuses are needed (for example `generating`, `awaiting_approval`, `running_tools`, `ready`, `failed`)?
   - Is status persisted in the thread structure, or reconstructed from messages and pending calls?
   - What should a reconnecting client see if generation or a tool is still running?

8. **UI**
   - Where do pending calls and results appear in the conversation?
   - What call details are shown before approval, and can arguments be inspected or edited?
   - Should approval controls exist only for the currently selected thread, or work from any subscribed client?

9. **Security and limits**
   - What filesystem/network access, timeouts, and output-size limits may tools have?
   - Should tool execution run in-process, or in a restricted worker/process?
   - Which arguments and results need validation or redaction before persistence/logging?

The core loop will be intentionally small: the model emits a `tool` code block containing YAML, the server parses it into `{ tool, args }`, runs the registered function, streams its output as a message, then asks the model to continue. ### Decisions made from your direction

- **Tool-call format:** tool calls are fenced code blocks tagged `tool`, with YAML content. Parse them from the completed model response into `{ tool, args }`.
- **Tool definition:** each registered tool has raw-text instructions for the model and a server-side function. Model output selects a tool by name; only registered tools can execute.
- **Message roles:** any message can be ongoing—LLM or tool output. Ongoing state is tracked in memory on the server as a set of message IDs per thread.
- **Thread activity:** broadcast `is_active` based on whether that thread has any ongoing messages. On restart or reconnect, activity should reflect actual in-memory work; persisted unfinished messages must not be treated as active.
- **Context building:** map `tool` messages to `user`, then combine adjacent messages with the same resulting role when building plain context for the LLM.
- **Thread structure:** change the current structure toward `drafts/archi thread.md`: tree/roots/focus, per-root config including enabled tools, messages, and thread metadata/status as needed.
- **Scope:** start with one simple, raw-capability tool (bash-like), keeping the code path straightforward. No general plugin system, approval UI, or provider adapter framework yet.

1. **Settle the minimum thread shape**

3. **Build context with tool instructions**

   - Convert `tool` messages to `user` messages for plain context.
   - Combine consecutive messages with the same role, preserving message order and separating content clearly.
   - Keep the existing user/assistant handling unchanged unless required by the new root/config shape.

4. **Implement ongoing-message tracking**
   - Maintain an in-memory set of ongoing message IDs per thread on the server.
   - Mark a message ongoing when its stream begins; remove it when it finishes, including error paths.
   - Broadcast `is_active` whenever the set changes.
   - On subscribe, send the current thread structure and its current in-memory active status.
   - Ensure a failed tool or model request cannot leave a message marked ongoing.

5. **Implement the tool loop**

## Revised plan

The backend remains the authority for thread state and tool execution. The frontend can confirm a pending call, but **for now every pending call is called automatically**. We’ll keep that boundary so confirmation UI can be added later without changing the tool protocol.

### 1. Adopt the planned thread structure

Change the current structure to the `archi thread` shape, in small increments:

- `tree`: nodes and their child/focus relationships.
- `roots`: root IDs mapped to config, including enabled tool names and pending tool calls.
- `messages`: message ID to message structure.
- Keep the active state derived from in-memory ongoing-message tracking on the server, rather than treating it as durable thread content.

No legacy file migration: existing thread data may not load under the new shape.

### 2. Define tool calls and pending state

- Parse fenced `tool` blocks from a completed assistant response as YAML.
- A parsed call has `{ tool, args }`; assign it a random ID when adding it to the root’s `pending_tools`.
- Keep the original YAML blocks in the assistant message content.
- Broadcast the updated pending calls so clients stay synchronized.
- Add a frontend action to call a pending tool by ID.
- When handling that action, pop the call from pending state. If its ID is missing, ignore it.

### 3. Execute calls sequentially and stream results

- Initially, when a pending call appears, the frontend automatically requests its execution.
- Execute calls one at a time, in pending order.
- Represent each execution as a `tool` message, using the existing message/tree/stream broadcasts.
- Track that message as ongoing while its output streams; clear it on finish or failure.
- Expose `is_active` based on whether the thread has any ongoing messages, and synchronize changes via broadcasts.

### 4. Build tool-aware LLM context

- Add each enabled tool’s raw-text instructions when building context.
- Map `tool` messages to `user` for the LLM.
- Combine consecutive messages that resolve to the same role.
- Preserve the assistant’s original tool YAML in its message content.

### 5. Resume generation from synchronized state

After a tool call is consumed and its tool message finishes, check the current thread state. Start the next generation only when the latest relevant message is a tool message and the thread is inactive, with no ongoing messages and no pending calls. This makes the continuation depend on synchronized state, not just a particular action’s control flow.

### 6. Wire up the UI and broadcasts

- Handle pending-tool and active-state broadcasts in `app.ts`.
- Automatically send the call action for each pending call.
- Initially render tool output as an ordinary message; no approval controls or specialized tool cards yet.

### 7. Keep the first version deliberately small

- Sequential execution only.
- One initial tool and a simple loop cap to avoid endless tool/generate cycles.
- No legacy migration, general plugin framework, parallel calls, or security work in this pass.

import { deserialize, serialize } from 'action/index'
import { init_desktop, data, touch, config, mkpath, join } from 'lib/file'

init_desktop('humility')

export const thread_index_file = data('chat', 'index.yaml')
export const config_file = config('chat', 'config.yaml')
export const env_file = config('chat', 'env.yaml')
touch(thread_index_file, serialize({}))
touch(config_file, serialize({}))
touch(env_file, serialize({}))

const thread_folder = data('chat', 'thread')
const thread_log_folder = data('chat', 'log', 'thread')
const message_log_folder = data('chat', 'log', 'message')
mkpath(thread_log_folder)
mkpath(message_log_folder)

export function get_thread_file(thread: id) {
  return join(thread_folder, thread)
}

export function get_thread_log_file(thread: id) {
  return join(thread_log_folder, `${thread}.jsonl`)
}

export function get_message_log_file(message: id) {
  return join(message_log_folder, `${message}.jsonl`)
}

export const server_log_file = data('chat', 'log', 'server', `server.log`)
touch(server_log_file)

--- list ---
import { deserialize, serialize, thread_index_file } from 'action/index'
import { read } from 'lib/file'

export function list() {
  return deserialize(read(thread_index_file))
}

--- hide ---
import { deserialize, serialize, thread_index_file } from 'action/index'
import { read, write } from 'lib/file'

export function hide({ thread }) {
  let thread_index: thread_index = deserialize(read(thread_index_file))

  thread_index[thread].is_hidden = true

  write(thread_index_file, serialize(thread_index))
}

from pathlib import Path

path = Path('../utility/tools.ts')
text = path.read_text().replace('return await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {', 'return await new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {')
path.write_text(text)

path = Path('../utility/thread.ts')
text = path.read_text().replace(
    'thread_structure.messages[message] = message_structure\n',
    'thread_structure.messages[message] = message_structure as message_structure\n',
)
path.write_text(text)

path = Path('../backend/serve.ts')
text = path.read_text()
text = text.replace(
    "import { parse_tool_calls, tool_registry, type tool_call } from 'utility/tools'",
    "import { parse_tool_calls, tool_registry, type tool_call as tool_call_structure } from 'utility/tools'",
)
text = text.replace('let tool_call: tool_call | undefined', 'let tool_call: tool_call_structure | undefined')
text = text.replace('let pending_tools: Record<id, tool_call> = {}', 'let pending_tools: Record<id, tool_call_structure> = {}')
text = text.replace('async function run_tool(thread: id, call: tool_call)', 'async function run_tool(thread: id, call: tool_call_structure)')
text = text.replace('function respond(request: id, payload: any, client: WebSocket) {\n  client.send(', "function respond(request: id, payload: any, client: WebSocket) {\n  append_server_log('respond', payload)\n\n  client.send(")
path.write_text(text)

path = Path('../utility/generate.ts')
text = path.read_text().replace('\n\n\n    return {', '\n\n    return {')
path.write_text(text)
PY

**Considering file management**

I'm thinking about our file management setup. We have primarily planned files and maybe just one additional file. I could avoid importing the thread utility from the tools by defining raw instructions in a separate text constant file, keeping it simple without node imports. The backend tools can handle those imports. It’s a more streamlined approach, which seems like a good way to keep things organized and efficient.

I’ll split browser-safe tool instructions/types into `utility/tools.ts` and move YAML parsing plus bash execution to a backend-only `backend/tools.ts`.

M ../backend/serve.ts
 M ../utility/generate.ts
 M ../utility/thread.ts
 M component/app.ts
?? ../backend/tools.ts
?? ../utility/tools.ts

content.text: Final inspection caught a name-shadowing bug in `build_plain_context`: the local instruction list shadowed the imported instruction map. I’ll rename the import and list so tool instructions resolve correctly.

arguments.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
path = Path('../utility/thread.ts')
text = path.read_text()
text = text.replace(
    "import { tool_instructions } from './tools'",
    "import { tool_instructions as tool_instruction_text } from './tools'",
)
text = text.replace(
    "  const tool_instructions = (root_config.tools ?? [])\n    .map((name) => tool_instructions[name])\n    .filter(Boolean)\n  const system_prompt = [root_config.system_prompt, ...tool_instructions]",
    "  const tool_instruction_list = (root_config.tools ?? [])\n    .map((name) => tool_instruction_text[name])\n    .filter(Boolean)\n  const system_prompt = [root_config.system_prompt, ...tool_instruction_list]",
)
text = text.replace(
    '  return build_path(thread_structure).map((node) => thread_structure.messages[node])',
    '  return build_path(thread_structure).map(\n    (node) => thread_structure.messages[node],\n  )',
)
path.write_text(text)
PY

git diff --check; sed -n '1,60p' ../utility/thread.ts

Implemented the YAML tool-calling loop.

- Added a backend bash tool that parses fenced `tool` YAML and streams command output into `tool` messages.
- Updated thread state to root configs with pending calls; LLM context includes tool instructions, maps tool messages to `user`, and combines adjacent same-role messages.
- Added server-side ongoing-message tracking and `is_active` / pending-call broadcasts.
- Updated the frontend to automatically call pending tools sequentially, then generate again when idle and the latest message is a tool result.
- Preserved the original YAML in assistant messages. Unknown pending-call IDs are ignored.
- No legacy thread migration. Bash runs through `bash -lc` without additional restrictions.

Changed files: `source/backend/serve.ts`, `source/backend/tools.ts` (new), `source/utility/generate.ts`, `source/utility/thread.ts`, `source/utility/tools.ts` (new), and `source/web/component/app.ts`.

I did not build or test, per project instructions.
add the bash tool on new thread template or fix logics to make it see such tool, or give it brief instruction to output proper tools when there is any.

New threads already enable `bash` in `empty_thread_structure()`, and `build_plain_context()` adds its instructions to the LLM context. I strengthened the instruction in `source/utility/tools.ts` to tell the model when to use tools and show the exact `tool`-tagged YAML format the parser expects.

`git diff --check` is clean. I did not build or test.
